ta-l1d15q5-d1e3498.summary: Transitional paragraph turning to mission in relation to those to whom it is made, in three articles: to whom the Son's or Spirit's mission is made; whether it was fuller after the incarnation than before; and whether invisible mission makes its recipients not be in this world.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3515.summary: First argument that mission is made to irrational creatures too. Mission is for sanctifying the creature, and some irrational creatures, such as the temple and vessels, are said to be sanctified.
claims: Temples and vessels are sanctified.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3518.summary: Second argument. Grace can be in nothing unless there is a mission to it, and grace is contained in the sacraments, which are insensible creatures.
claims: Grace is contained in the sacraments.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3521.summary: Third argument. The Son proceeds not only as the Word manifesting the Father by knowledge but also as representing the Father by likeness of nature. All creatures, even insensible ones, bear a likeness of the Son's generation by proceeding in imitation of the divine nature through participated attributes, as the rational creature resembles him as Word by participating wisdom. So as the Son is sent to rational creatures as Word, he should be sent to irrational ones as Son.
claims: All creatures imitate the divine nature and so resemble the Son's generation.
concepts: likeness of the Son in creatures

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3524.summary: Sed contra. Mission of a divine person is only by sanctifying grace, of which only rational creatures are capable.
claims: Only rational creatures are capable of sanctifying grace.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3533.summary: Further question: whether the Son or Spirit is said to be sent to all saints by an increase of grace. It seems not, since mission implies a new mode of the person's existence in the creature, and by increase of grace God is not said to be in the saints in another way than before.
claims: Increase of grace does not give God a new mode of presence.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3536.summary: Second argument. Mission is to call back the rational creature, as Lombard says, and only those who stray are called back. The saints do not stray.
claims: Mission recalls those who stray.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3539.summary: Sed contra. The Spirit was sent to the apostles at Pentecost in a visible mission, and visible mission shows invisible mission. They already had grace, so the persons are said to be sent to the saints by an increase of grace.
claims: The Pentecost mission was to those who already had grace.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3548.summary: Further question: whether the Spirit's mission is made to angels and the other blessed. It seems not, since mission is always by some effect of grace, and in those who have reached the end grace is neither newly given nor increased.
claims: The blessed receive no new or increased grace.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3551.summary: Second argument. The messenger and the one to whom the mission is made are not the same, and angels act as messengers in the missions of Son and Spirit, guarding and suggesting. So no mission is made to them, otherwise there would be an infinite regress.
claims: Angels are messengers of the divine missions.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3564.summary: Further question: whether a mission can be made to Christ as man. It seems not, since mission is always to something distant, and Christ's human nature was never distant from the divine, being united to it and full of all grace from his conception.
claims: Mission is to something distant.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3567.summary: Second argument. Mission is for sanctifying the creature, and what is sanctified is what is not holy, but Christ was never not holy.
claims: Only what is not holy is sanctified.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3570.summary: Sed contra. The Spirit's mission is his giving, and the Spirit was given to Christ: 'God does not give the Spirit by measure' (John 3:34).
claims: The Spirit was given to Christ.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3576.summary: Second sed contra. Visible mission is a sign of invisible mission, and a visible mission of the Spirit was made to Christ in the form of a dove (Matt. 3).
claims: The dove at Christ's baptism was a visible mission.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3585.summary: Thomas's answer to the first sub-question. Since mission of a divine person is only in gifts of sanctifying grace, it is made only to those who can receive such gifts: to all rational creatures, except those depraved by obstinacy in evil, such as demons and the damned, and not to irrational creatures.
claims: Mission is made to rational creatures capable of sanctifying grace, not to irrational creatures, demons, or the damned.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3588.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Sanctify' is said in three ways: as cleansing from sin by grace (holy as clean), as confirming in good by grace or glory (holy as firm), both of which occur only in rational creatures and alone involve mission; and as setting something apart for divine worship, which befits all cleanness, in which sense temple and vessels are sanctified.
claims: Only cleansing and confirming sanctification involve mission; consecration of things does not.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3591.summary: Reply to the second argument. Grace is in the sacraments not as in its subject but as in the instrument by which grace is conferred (Book IV, Dist. 1). So the sacraments' sanctification belongs to the third mode, which involves no mission.
claims: Sacraments contain grace instrumentally, not as subject.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3594.summary: Reply to the third argument. Mission belongs to the creature's return to its end, so it can be only by what can imply relation to the end. The Son's generation, as Son, is said only by going out from the principle, so in that respect it pertains not to mission but to creation, by which things are brought into being, since all things were made through the Son. The concepts of Word and love relate to both, so they pertain to creation and to mission. Also, the imitation of divine nature that the Son receives perfectly is shared by the first effects by which we subsist in natural being, which are not enough for the union mission requires.
claims: The Son as Son relates to creation; as Word, together with love, he relates to both creation and mission.
Natural likeness to God does not suffice for mission, which concerns return to the end.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3598.summary: Concedes the sed contra of the first sub-question.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3607.summary: Thomas's answer to the second sub-question. The Son and Spirit are said to be sent to the saints by an increase of grace. An increase may be only in the intensity of the same virtue, which is not called a new mission, or it may perfect the person for a new use or act of grace, which is a new mission. For example, knowledge of God from which love proceeds suffices for the Son's mission, but when knowledge is raised by inspiration to know divine mysteries, it is given in the gift of prophecy. Likewise any charity suffices for the Spirit's mission, but when love grows so that another use of grace is conferred through it, such as working miracles or overcoming every temptation without difficulty, there is a new mission. Others say there is a mission in every increase of sanctifying grace, which can also easily be held.
claims: New missions occur when increased grace perfects one for a new use or act, such as prophecy or miracles.
It can also be held that every increase of sanctifying grace is a mission.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3610.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although there is no new general mode, there is a special mode, insofar as the person likens the recipient to himself by a special use of grace. Or he is there in a fuller way, which suffices for mission on the second opinion.
claims: A new special use or a fuller presence suffices for a new mission.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3613.summary: Reply to the second argument. Recalling the straying belongs to mission only incidentally, on the side of a recipient in sin. Mission determines its terminus ad quem, that grace be conferred, but not its terminus a quo, whether the state of sin, of mere nature, or of lesser grace. Alternatively, though it does not actually recall one straying, grace keeps one from straying, which is a kind of recall from error.
claims: Mission determines its terminus ad quem (grace) but not its terminus a quo.
concepts: terminus a quo and ad quem

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3622.summary: Thomas's answer to the third sub-question. The vision essential to beatitude, charity, and whatever pertains to the substantial reward do not increase in angels and the blessed once they are blessed. But new revelations can still be made to them, since however perfect their knowledge, God's knowledge exceeds it infinitely, and by these revelations they rise to the love of God, not loving more but with their love directed to God under another aspect.
claims: Substantial beatitude does not increase, but the blessed receive new revelations that redirect their love under new aspects.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3625.summary: Reply to the first argument. The Son and Spirit were sent to the angels in the conferral of grace or glory, and they are sent to them further, after they become blessed, by new revelations and new ways of loving. Though there is no mission by intensive increase of grace, there is one insofar as their grace is in a way increased extensively to more things through new revelations.
claims: Missions to the blessed occur by extensive, not intensive, increase of grace.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3628.summary: Reply to the second argument. In the same mission the messenger and the recipient are not the same, but in different missions there is no difficulty. In the divine persons' mission to us, angels are messengers not by entering the mind but by external ministry. In the mission to angels they are not messengers, except perhaps as higher angels cooperate with the divine persons in illuminating lower ones. There is no infinite regress, since one reaches the highest angels, who receive the light of divine revelation immediately.
claims: Angels serve the missions to us by external ministry, and the regress ends at the highest angels, who receive revelation immediately.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3637.summary: Thomas's answer to the fourth sub-question. The Son of God was undoubtedly sent to the human nature in Christ by the visible mission into flesh. Whether the Son was sent to Christ as man invisibly, or the Spirit visibly or invisibly, is doubtful. Some say no invisible mission was made to him, since he was full of grace from his conception and his grace never increased; the Spirit's visible mission to him manifested his inner grace, not a new interior mission. Others say, more truly, that an invisible mission was made to Christ's soul in the conferral of grace at his conception, but none afterward, since his grace was never renewed.
claims: An invisible mission was made to Christ's soul at his conception, but none afterward, since his grace never increased.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3640.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although the human nature did not exist in time before the union, it is prior in understanding to consider it in itself than as united, so the Son is sent to it by the grace of union, the mission into flesh. Also, even as united, it is distant from the divine nature in its natural condition, though not in unity of person, so an invisible mission by grace into the mind can be made to the human nature even as united, though the nature does not precede grace in time.
claims: The human nature, prior in understanding and distant in natural condition, can receive mission by the grace of union and by habitual grace.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3643.summary: Reply to the second argument. To sanctify is to make holy, either from not-holy or from holy. From not-holy privatively, when something apt for holiness lacks it, does not fit Christ. From not-holy negatively fits Christ in his human nature, which was not holy before it existed, and this suffices for mission. From holy to holier also preserves the concept of mission but does not fit Christ. Sanctification as continuation in holiness is not said properly and does not suffice for mission, since there is no newness, though it fits Christ ('for them I sanctify myself', John 17:19).
claims: Christ's human nature was sanctified 'from not-holy' negatively, which suffices for mission.
Continuation in holiness, which Christ has, involves no newness and is not mission.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3649.summary: Reply to the first sed contra on the other opinion: not every giving is a mission, only giving to something pre-existing, though this has little reason behind it.
claims: On the rejected view, only giving to something pre-existing is mission.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3653.summary: The reply to the second sed contra is evident from the body.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3666.summary: First argument that invisible mission was not fuller after the incarnation than before. Mission is a kind of radiation of divine goodness in sanctifying gifts, and the bodily sun, to which Dionysius likens divine goodness, always radiates equally.
claims: Divine goodness, like the sun, radiates equally always.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3669.summary: Second argument. Augustine says John's celibacy is not preferred to Abraham's marriage, so the New Testament saints are not of greater merit than the Old. The fullness of mission is measured by abundance of grace, the principle of merit. Also, Old Testament saints are proposed as examples of perfect virtue (Heb. 11), such as Job's patience and Abraham's faith.
claims: Old Testament saints are not less in merit than New Testament saints.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3672.summary: Sed contra from Augustine on John 7:39, 'the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified': this means the giving or mission of the Spirit was to be such as had never been before. It existed before, but not such.
claims: After Christ's glorification the Spirit was given as never before.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3682.summary: Thomas's determination. Mission can be considered on the side of the sender, in whom there is no change, so it is equal at all times, except as by the predetermination of his wisdom and foreknowledge he preordained, without changing, to do something at one time and not another according to the fittingness of times. Or it can be considered on the side of the recipients, and then those better prepared to receive grace receive fuller grace. Through Christ's coming the obstacle of the ancient condemnation was removed, and the whole human race was made readier to receive grace, both by the payment of the price and the victory over the devil and by Christ's teaching, through which divine things are known more clearly. So, speaking generally, mission was fuller after the incarnation, since from his fullness we have all received. But to some particular persons in the Old Testament the fullest mission was made in perfection of virtue, and they too received from Christ's fullness, being saved by faith in the mediator (Augustine).
claims: On the sender's side, mission is equal at all times; on the recipients' side, it is fuller after the incarnation.
Christ's redemption and teaching made humanity better prepared to receive grace.
Some Old Testament saints had the fullest mission, but through faith in Christ the mediator.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3685.summary: Reply to the first argument. The argument concerns the sender, who in himself always stands equally toward conferring grace.
claims: The sender is equally disposed at all times.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3688.summary: Reply to the second argument. Old Testament saints can be considered as to personal grace, in which by faith in the mediator they obtained grace as full as New Testament saints, many more and many less, or as to the state of nature at that time. In the latter respect, since they were still bound by the divine sentence for the first parent's sin and the price was not yet paid, there was an impediment, so that mission was not made to them as fully as in the New Testament, including the passage into glory, in which every imperfection of nature is removed.
claims: As to personal grace, Old Testament saints could equal New Testament saints; as to the state of nature, they were impeded by the unpaid debt of original sin.
concepts: personal grace vs. state of nature

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3700.summary: First argument that invisible mission makes us not be in this world. Whoever is in heaven is not in the world, and the Apostle says for all the saints, 'our conversation is in heaven' (Phil. 3:20).
claims: Our conversation is in heaven.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3706.summary: Second argument. Augustine says the soul is more truly where it loves than where it is. To be essentially in something is the truest way of being in it, so the saints are essentially in the heavenly things they love.
claims: The soul is more truly where it loves.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3709.summary: Third argument. The soul, an incorporeal substance, is determined to a place only accidentally, so it is essentially wherever it is accidentally. It is accidentally in its object as in its matter, so it is essentially where its object is.
claims: The soul is in place only accidentally.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3713.summary: Fourth argument. We say angels are in a place because they operate there, and the soul's operation is about its object, so the soul is essentially where its object is.
claims: Angels are where they operate.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3716.summary: Sed contra. A form never exceeds that whose form it is, and the soul is the essential form of the body, so it is essentially only where the body is, and the body is never outside the world while we live.
claims: The soul as form is essentially where the body is.
concepts: soul as form of the body

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3719.summary: Thomas's determination. Our soul relates to two things: to the body, to which it gives substantial being, by which it also itself exists (the soul's being is just what it gives the body, Dist. 8), and to its object, from which it receives being according to second perfection, accidental being. So the soul is essentially where its body is, to which it has an essential relation, and is where its object is not essentially but by a kind of conformity, as knowledge is the assimilation of the knower to the known. That is how Lombard's text means that 'insofar as we grasp something eternal with the mind we are not in this world': our affection and intellect are conformed not to worldly, perishing things but to heavenly and eternal ones. The Apostle's 'our conversation is in heaven' is to be understood the same way.
claims: The soul is essentially where its body is and is 'in' its object only by conformity of knowledge and love.
Invisible mission removes us from the world by conforming intellect and affection to eternal things.
concepts: being in heaven by love and knowledge

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3728.summary: The reply to the first argument follows from this.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3731.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although the soul's substantial being lies in its union with the body, its whole nobility lies in being joined to its perfections by its noblest acts. So Augustine says the soul is more truly where it loves, since it is there by its nobler being, according to its ultimate perfection.
claims: The soul is 'more truly' where it loves according to its ultimate perfection, not its substantial being.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3734.summary: Reply to the third argument. Place belongs to the soul only accidentally, but to be essentially in a place it must also be essentially joined to that by reason of which place is attributed to it. The soul is not essentially joined to its object but only through a received likeness of it: the stone is not in the soul, but its species (the Philosopher), and the soul is joined to that species or intention not as to its first, substantial being but as to its second, accidental being. So the soul is not essentially in a place by reason of its object.
claims: The soul is joined to its object only by a received species, as to accidental being, not essentially.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3738.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. An angel's operation on bodily things is active, so it must be joined by its power, inseparable from its essence, to the body it acts on, as mover to moved. The intellectual soul's operation on what it knows and loves is not active but receptive, so it need not be essentially joined to it, only receive its intention.
claims: Angelic operation on bodies is active and requires conjunction; the soul's knowing and loving are receptive.

ta-l1d15q5-d1e3748.summary: An expositio textus. (1) The Son could be called sent in that, being from the Father, he is apt to be sent by him, so mission is understood by aptitude rather than act. (2) 'He is sent to each when he is known by someone' means not only speculative but quasi-experiential knowledge, as the addition 'and perceived' shows, which signifies experience in the gift received. (3) The rational soul is said to advance toward God in this life and to be perfected in God in heaven, where both missions will be completed by perfect knowledge and perfect love. (4) 'How he is sent daily to the saints' means not that a mission is made daily to one who has grace but that no time is fixed to which divine liberality is restricted. (5) 'The Father is the principle of the whole divinity' can be read as concerning the perfection of deity, so that the Father is principle of the Son, in whom deity is perfect, but this does not fit Augustine's meaning, since then the Son too would be principle of the whole divinity. Better, it concerns the totality of the persons in number: the Father is the principle in all the divine persons, not of himself, as a foundation is the principle of the whole house though not of itself. 'Principle of deity' is better than 'of divinity', since 'divinity' implies participated deity.
claims: Mission involves quasi-experiential knowledge of the person in the perceived gift.
Both missions will be completed in heaven by perfect knowledge and love.
The Father is 'principle of the whole divinity' as principle in all the persons, not of himself.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3510.summary: Sub-question 1 asks whether mission is made to irrational creatures, given that temples and vessels are sanctified, sacraments contain grace, and all creatures resemble the Son's generation. The sed contra limits mission to those capable of sanctifying grace.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3528.summary: Sub-question 2 asks whether the persons are sent to the saints by an increase of grace, weighing the lack of a new mode of presence and the absence of straying against the Pentecost mission to the apostles.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3543.summary: Sub-question 3 asks whether mission is made to angels and the blessed, who receive no new grace and themselves serve as messengers.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3559.summary: Sub-question 4 asks whether mission can be made to Christ as man, whose human nature was never distant from the divine and was always holy, against the giving of the Spirit without measure and the dove at the baptism.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3580.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 1 holds that mission is made to rational creatures capable of sanctifying grace, excluding irrational creatures and the obstinate (demons, the damned). The sanctification of temples and vessels is consecration for worship, not mission, and sacraments contain grace instrumentally. The Son as Son relates to creation, as Word to both creation and mission.
claims: Mission is made only to rational creatures capable of sanctifying grace.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3602.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 2 holds that the persons are sent to the saints by an increase of grace that perfects them for a new use or act, such as prophecy, miracles, or easy victory over temptation, though it can also be held that every increase is a mission. Mission determines its terminus ad quem, not its terminus a quo.
claims: New missions to the saints occur through increase of grace for new uses.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3617.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 3 holds that missions were made to the angels in the gift of grace and glory and continue by new revelations that extend their grace to more objects, without increasing substantial beatitude. Angels minister externally in missions to us, and the hierarchy ends at the highest angels, who are illumined immediately.
claims: Missions to the blessed continue by new revelations, an extensive increase of grace.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3632.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 4 holds, as the truer view, that an invisible mission was made to Christ's soul at his conception and none afterward, since his grace never increased. The human nature, distant from the divine in its natural condition, could receive both the grace of union and habitual grace, and it was sanctified 'from not-holy' negatively.
claims: An invisible mission was made to Christ's soul at conception only.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 5 introduces mission in relation to its recipients, in three articles: to whom it is made, whether it was fuller after the incarnation, and whether it removes its recipients from the world.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3502.summary: Article 1 asks to whom mission is made. Its four sub-questions hold that mission is made only to rational creatures capable of sanctifying grace, and to the saints whenever increased grace perfects them for a new use. It continues to the blessed and the angels through new revelations, an extensive increase of grace. It was made to Christ's soul invisibly at his conception and not afterward, since his fullness of grace never increased.
claims: Mission is made to rational creatures capable of grace, to the saints by new uses of grace, to the blessed by new revelations, and to Christ at his conception.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3658.summary: Article 2 asks whether mission was fuller after the incarnation. On the sender's side it is always equal, but on the recipients' side it is fuller after the incarnation, since Christ's redemption and teaching removed the obstacle of the ancient condemnation and prepared humanity for grace. Some Old Testament saints received the fullest mission in personal virtue, through faith in the mediator, but were impeded in the state of nature until the price was paid.
claims: Mission is fuller after the incarnation, by the recipients' greater preparation through Christ.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3692.summary: Article 3 asks whether invisible mission makes us not be in this world. The soul is essentially where its body is, as its form, and is in its objects only by conformity of knowledge and love, which concerns second, accidental being. So mission removes us from the world not in place but by conforming intellect and affection to eternal things, and the soul is 'more truly where it loves' according to its ultimate perfection.
claims: Invisible mission removes us from the world by conforming knowledge and love to eternal things, not by relocating the soul.

ta-l1d15q5-Dd1e3743.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 15 explains mission by aptitude and the quasi-experiential knowledge it involves. It notes that both missions are completed in heaven and that no fixed time restricts divine liberality, and interprets the Father as principle of the whole divinity in the sense of being principle in all the persons.
claims: The Father is principle in all the persons, not of himself.

ta-l1d15q5.summary: Quaestio 5 of Book I, Distinction 15 treats mission in relation to its recipients. Article 1 holds that mission is made only to rational creatures capable of sanctifying grace. New missions occur to the saints when grace is increased for a new use, to the blessed and angels through new revelations, and to Christ's soul once, at his conception, since his fullness of grace never increased. Article 2 holds that mission, though always equal on God's side, became fuller after the incarnation on the recipients' side, because Christ's redemption and teaching prepared humanity for grace. Old Testament saints were saved by faith in the mediator. Article 3 holds that mission removes us from the world not by relocating the soul, which is essentially where its body is, but by conforming knowledge and love to eternal things.
claims: Mission is made only to rational creatures capable of grace, and recurs with new uses of grace and new revelations.
Mission became fuller after the incarnation through humanity's greater preparation.
Mission removes us from the world by conformity of intellect and affection, not by place.
